note: para 209: holding is that CCK (established under KICA 1998) lawfully existed and its actions were not rendered unconstitutional by the 2010 Constitution pending transition; a transitional ruling on the regulator, not a challenge to s.5 as such ('CCK had a lawful existence, and its actions were not unconstitutional', para 206)

para 39: SC declined jurisdiction ('even as we down our tools', para 38) and only restates its own 2021 Muruatetu directions for posterity: 'We say no more,save to recapitulate that our decision in the Muruatetu case did not generally invalidate...'; no new holding (duplicates E08)
para 39: same restatement of the Muruatetu directions as event 478; s.203 is the offence section, not a sentencing provision ruled on; petition dismissed for want of jurisdiction (para 40)

para 77: SC's own construction: 'section 193A of the Criminal Procedure Code cannot be invoked to aid that unlawful course of action'; s.193A is a single rule construed as a whole, so scope arguably total

no para numbers (end of judgment): challenge to Act 3 of 1969 amending CPC s.7 to let first-class magistrates pass any sentence for s.296 offences rejected: 'We can see no valid ground for assuming that the said amendment was contrary to the Constitution'; only the s.296-sentencing power was challenged, so partial

final paras (unnumbered): CA extends Muruatetu to s.296(2) on its own reasoning: 'We do not see any reason why this approach should not be applied to the mandatory sentence of death specified by section 296 (2)'; matter remitted for resentencing; same pattern as E11 (read_down)

para 34: plain construction of the s.8(5) defence, not constitutionally driven: 'the elements constituting the defence should be read disjunctively if the two sub-sections are to make sense' -> interpreted, not read_down

para 11: CA merely follows SC Mwangi ('We are bound by the decision of the Supreme Court') and para 13 says the constitutionality issue, raised for the first time, 'does not therefore fall for our determination'

para 11: 'we allow the appellant's appeal against sentence to the extent of finding that the mandatory nature of the sentence of life imprisonment provided under Section 8(2) ... is unconstitutional, as is the indeterminate term'; same type as E12 Manyeso

para 23-24: CA's own finding, though not repeated in the orders (para 25): 'would agree that just as the powers vested under section 25 of the Penal Code, the powers vested under section 166 of the CPC is unconstitutional'; para 24 limits it to 'the powers given to the President to order detention' -> partial

para 22: CA's own holding that Muruatetu's ratio 'on the unconstitutional nature of mandatory death sentences ... equally applies mutatis mutandis ... to the mandatory nature of death sentences ... under Section 296 (2)'; 'it cannot be said that the mandatory nature ... is unconstitutional in one section ... and constitutional in another'. Borderline with read_down (cf. E11 wording)

para 13-14: CA rejects HC's view that 'the death sentence has been abolished by the New Constitution' ('It was not ... Article 26 (3) did save the death penalty') and sets aside HC's substitution, reinstating death under s.296(2). Acts on the HC judgment below; if the HC statement is not stored as an event, 'upheld' would be the fallback type
para 31-32: no own reasoning, simply relies on SC Mwangi ('the Supreme Court clarified that the death sentence under Section 296(2) ... remains valid'); sentence confirmed as prescribed

unnumbered, end: HC rejects the constitutional challenge to the death sentence: 'On the issue of the sentence being unconstitutional, we wish to state that this is not true. The Constitution in Article 26 (3) allows deprivation of life'; brief, leans on Mwaura; only s.296(2) was at issue -> partial

para 16: 'We have addressed our minds to the issue of death sentence being unconstitutional ... it remains the mandatory sentence as under section 296(2)'; challenge rejected on Art 26 reasoning; only 296(2) ruled on -> partial (subsection given but scope says total)

para 33 is the holding: 'The deprivation of liberty sanctioned by sections 38 and 40 of the Civil Procedure Act is permissible and is not in violation of either the Constitution or the ICCPR'; quoted para 34 is only about the petitioner's execution process; only committal (s.38(d)/proviso) was challenged -> partial

Declarations and Orders 1: 'We hereby declare that Sections 295, 296(1), 296(2), 297(1) and 297(2) ... do not meet the constitutional threshold'; covers all of s.297; declaration suspended 18 months (order 3)

Declarations and Orders 1 (duplicate copy of Kahinga, Pet 618 of 2010): 'We hereby declare that Sections 295, 296(1), 296(2), 297(1) and 297(2) ... do not meet the constitutional threshold'; suspended 18 months (order 3)

Declarations and Orders 1 (Kahinga): covers 296(1) and 296(2), i.e. all of s.296; court also held death sentence not mandatory ('it is not mandatory for the courts to pass a death sentence'), which could be stored as a separate read_down of 296(2)
para 37: 'I am unable to hold that the proviso to section 124 is discriminatory, unconstitutional or that it violates articles 25 and 27'; only the proviso challenged -> partial

para 53(a): 'A declaration that trial courts are enjoined by section 333(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, in imposing sentences, other than sentence of death to take account of the period spent in custody'
para 53(c): 'A declaration that section 333(2) applies to the original sentence as well as the sentence imposed during resentencing'
para 307 (second '307'): 'section 6 of KICA as amended by Statute Law (Miscellaneous Amendment) Act No. 18 of 2018 is unconstitutional, null and void'; repeated in final declaration I
para 153(b): 'sections 162(4) and (5), 166 (2)...(7) and 167(1)(a), (b), (2), (3) and (4) ... Such provisions are hereby declared unconstitutional, null and void'; 162(4),(5) only -> partial
para 153(b): same order, s.166(2)-(7) declared 'unconstitutional, null and void'; 166(1) untouched -> partial
para 153(b): same order, s.167(1)(a),(b),(2),(3),(4) declared 'unconstitutional, null and void' -> partial

para 221: petition turned on CPC s.89(4)/(5) (paras 14, 43, 45); court holds the ODPP and NPS Acts 'supersede any provision of the Criminal Procedure Code ... which may give the impression that police officers are the persons to draft charge sheets and present them directly to courts'; only the charging power (89(4)-(5)) construed -> partial

para 38(a),(d),(g): 'To the extent that the provisions of sections 8(2), (3), (4), 11(1), 20(1) and 3(3) ... deprive the court the discretion ... the said provisions offend ... article 50(1)'; 'to the extent' form -> partial; para 36 notes minimum sentences 'not per se unconstitutional'

para 19: 'I find that the extent that the Sexual Offences Act prescribes minimum mandatory sentences with no discretion ... falls foul of article 28'; a finding of partial unconstitutionality (not a narrowing construction), raised suo motu, applied to the s.8(3) sentence (child aged 13)

para 30 (repeated para 35): ss.39(2)/(3) 'patently conflicting and may ... amount to discriminatory and disproportionate sentencing hence violating Article 51'; 'I declare that the period of long term rehabilitation, where the remainder of the sentence is less than 5 years, can only be for the remainder of the term'

para 31: under Sixth Schedule s.7 'I must construe this section with such modifications ... to bring into conformity with the Constitution. Thus, I take the minimum sentence to be indicative'; applied in para 38 (15 years imposed below the 20-year minimum of s.8(3))

para 71: 'whether section 63 of the Civil Procedure Act applies to these proceedings, the short answer is that it does not'; but the court adds it 'is not the law upon which the applicant's application turns ... of no consequence', so at best an obiter applicability ruling

para 16: s.5(2) 'shall be liable' and 'not less than' ambiguity resolved so 'the accused is entitled to the benefit of the least severe'; para 18 adds the Art 28 finding; minimum treated as non-mandatory (5 years imposed, para 19)
para 49(a): 'A declaration be and is hereby made that the mandatory nature of the death penalty as provided for under Section 296(2) and 279(2) of the Penal Code is unconstitutional'

para 40: 'I find merit in the contention ... that the mandatory nature of the death sentences provided for in Sections 296(2) and 297(2) of the Penal Code is unconstitutional'; order 49(a) says '279(2)', an evident typo for 297(2) (scope_text copies the typo)
para 140(a): 'A declaration is hereby issued that, section 77(1) and (3)(a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), and (g) of the Penal Code, cap 63 is unconstitutional'

para 53-54: conviction quashed (para 55), so the sentence remark is moot; the court only restates the Muruatetu directions: 'The decision of the Supreme Court did not extend the minimum mandatory sentence contemplated in the Sexual Offences Act'

para 50-51: quotes SC Mwangi paras 63-68 at length, then 'The foregoing elaborate findings of the Supreme Court are self-explanatory ... unless and until Section 8 ... is specifically declared unconstitutional ... it remains good law'; no independent holding
para 93(a): 'A declaration is hereby made that Section 226 of the Penal Code is unconstitutional for violating Articles 27, 28 and 43'; whole section -> total

para 83-84 / order (d): the constitutional challenge and declaration concern Rule 25 of the Small Claims Court Rules; 'arrest and committal under the Civil Procedure Act in itself is not unconstitutional' is a passing remark in declining damages, not a ruling on an impugned CPA s.40
